stories.headline: MLB playoffs 2026: First-look preview of division series matchups
stories.summary: The ALDS and NLDS are starting to take shape. Here's who has the edge -- and who should be on upset watch.
stories.body:
The 2026 MLB division series matchups are starting to take shape with the Chicago White Sox becoming the first team to advance out of the wild-card round on Wednesday.

Chicago's sweep of the Houston Astros sets up a division series with the Guardians, starting Saturday in Cleveland. The New York Yankees followed with a sweep of the Boston Red Sox, setting up an AL East showdown with the Tampa Bay Rays.

What have we learned about each team so far? What does each remaining club need to do to move on to the League Championship Series? Which players could be their teams' October difference-makers? And which favorites should be on upset watch in the round ahead?

Our ESPN MLB experts are here to break it all down as every division series matchup is set.

ALDS: New York Yankees vs. Tampa Bay Rays

Upset forecast: (Yankees win 55% of simulations) This number was calculated with the assumption that Aaron Judge will be a full go for the division series round. While that remains uncertain, the number drops to roughly 52% if he's out or reduced to a pinch-hitting role. That is to say the Yankees would be favored by the simulations either way. The Yankees held more than a five-win edge by Pythagorean record during the season. They also hold a 4.6-win edge in my postseason roster ratings.

That explains the probability but when you look at the different roster groups, you can see how this is a match of strengths against strengths. Both teams have excellent offenses, though they go about things in a polar opposite way, strong playoff rotations and versatile, high-performing bullpens. If the Rays keep the Yankees' power hitters in the yard, this probability probably flips.

Rays concern level: Bring it on. The Yankees may have an on-paper edge, but the Rays' roster and the way Kevin Cash deploys it stacks up against anybody. This the best possible matchup on the AL side in terms of roster ratings. So if you want to think of this as the real ALCS, it's not a hard position to defend. -- Doolittle

New York Yankees
What impressed you most about the Yankees in the wild-card round?

The Yankees' young homegrown players. Cam Schlittler and Ben Rice are franchise cornerstones who have come out of nowhere to become two of the best players in baseball -- and they shined in Game 1 -- but New York's ancillary draft-and-developed pieces also played their roles well.

The Yankees had four other homegrown players 27 or younger start at least one of the first two games and contribute in the wild-card round. Shortstop George Lombard Jr. -- the youngest of the group at 21 years old -- went 3-for-4 with two runs scored in his postseason debut in Game 1. Second baseman -- and former shortstop -- Anthony Volpe, outfielder Spencer Jones, and catcher Austin Wells each contributed with hits in the rout.

For the Yankees to make a deep October run without Aaron Judge -- their best homegrown player since the Core Four Era -- they'll need their young core to continue to make an impact.

Why will it/won't it continue against the Rays?

It'll continue because Schlittler and Rice aren't just neat stories anymore -- they're bona fide stars -- and the supporting cast will build on that wild-card round experience. The Rays pitching staff is among the elite in baseball, but so was Boston's. The group, playing with the heightened pressure that comes with a three-game series at Yankee Stadium, did not wither. Playing at Tropicana Field, where the Rays have one of baseball's best home-field advantages, will be a challenge, but the younger Yankees appear ready.

Which one player must deliver for New York to pull off the upset?

Judge's status for the series remains unclear. Even if the three-time MVP plays, expecting vintage Judge to immediately emerge is a stretch. So, with that, Rice is the Yankees' most important player.

He became the hitter that opposing teams game planned around with Judge sidelined for most of the regular season. The change coincided with his production nosediving. Rice was slashing .306/.397/.658 with 17 home runs in 54 games through May 31 -- the final game Judge played before going on the injured list with a fractured rib. From there, he slashed .216/.314/.432 with 18 home runs in 78 games through the end of August. Then he caught fire again, collecting nine hits in five games before Judge returned from the injured list Sept. 8. Eight days later, Judge strained his right calf, but Rice didn't stop hitting, going 9-for-31 with three home runs, two doubles, and a 1.120 OPS over his final nine regular season games to finish with 41 home runs and an .897 OPS.

Rice made the adjustments to fuel the Yankees' lineup. They'll need him to continue thriving to extend their season. -- Jorge Castillo

Tampa Bay Rays
What carried the Rays to an October bye?

Remarkable consistency. They were .500 or better in every month and finished strong, going 34-19 over the final two months. Drew Rasmussen and Nick Martinez were both All-Stars and the most underrated 1-2 combo in the majors, combining for 31 wins while ranking fourth and sixth in the AL in ERA. Trade deadline acquisition Freddy Peralta turned his season around after joining the Rays, giving them an excellent No. 3 starter with Shane McClanahan injured.

As always, the Rays play good defense, plus Junior Caminero and his 42 home runs anchor a lineup that led the majors with a .283 average with runners in scoring position.

Finally, Bryan Baker had an outstanding season as the closer, ranking fourth among all relievers in win probability added, and the bullpen as a whole was clutch all season as the Rays went 25-14 in one-run games.

Why will it/won't it continue against the Yankees?

Defense and pitching -- in a postseason that projects as a low-scoring October in the first place - will work no matter the opponent. Rasmussen isn't a household name, but he had nine starts this season where he allowed no runs and another seven where he allowed just one. Peralta is a huge key and he enters the postseason on a roll, with a 0.79 ERA over his final six starts (the Rays won all six games).

Yes, the Rays will need to get some of those big hits with runners on base, but they've done it all season and they excel at small ball -- leading the majors in sacrifice bunts and bunt hits -- and while you can't win exclusively scoring runs that way, it could be the difference in one game in a series.

Which one player must deliver to put Tampa Bay in the ALCS?

To that point, the Rays will need to hit some home runs along the way and Caminero is obviously the best bet to do that. He's just the second player along with Eddie Mathews with two 40-homer seasons through age 22, but he was a better all-around hitter this season than 2025, improving his OBP from .311 to .360 as he nearly doubled his walk rate. That maturity in his approach bodes well for a big postseason. -- David Schoenfield

ALDS: Chicago White Sox vs. Cleveland Guardians

Upset forecast: (Guardians win 57% of simulations) Though Chicago led the AL Central for the bulk of the season, Cleveland once again looked like the class of the mediocre division by season's end. The White Sox owned a better regular-season run differential, but the Guardians entered the postseason on one of their signature September heaters.

Both teams rely on an inordinate amount of production from rookies. As good as the White Sox's first-year players have been, no club can match what the Guardians have gotten from Parker Messick, Chase DeLauter, Travis Bazzana and others. Cleveland was the hotter team at the end of the regular season, and this is another series where home advantage might matter. That's not because the Guardians were that good at home but because the White Sox struggled so much on the road, ranking 20th in wins and run differential away from Rate Field.

Guardians concern level: Sky high. For a team with so many young players, the Guardians are dragging a lot of historical baggage. Some of that is historical (no titles since 1948) but more of it is recent. Cleveland keeps getting into the playoffs but with each run that falls short of the World Series, the pressure mounts. Meanwhile, no team left in the playoffs is playing with as much house money as the White Sox. -- Bradford Doolittle

Chicago White Sox

What impressed you most about the White Sox in the wild-card round?

The same thing that impressed me about them all season: their bullpen. It was masterful in their Game 1 victory and did enough after that to secure the series win. It's about as close as you'll come to a staff with every pitcher trained to pitch multiple innings every time out. Manager Will Venable has taken advantage of that all year, and it continued in the wild-card round.

Why will/won't it continue against the Guardians?

With time to rest before the ALDS starts Saturday and then three days off within the series, there is no reason the White Sox can't continue to lean on that pen. I might not have the same feelings if they advance to the ALCS -- at some point they'll run out of gas -- but the familiarity with the Guardians will also work to their advantage. The bullpen carrying it for one more round is a real possibility for Chicago.

Which one player must deliver for Chicago to keep its run going?

It's a tough call with so many options to choose from, but Hagen Smith has been lights out since coming up and he is less of a known commodity than others on the staff. And with those days off in the division series, Smith could impact up to three games.

The easier answer to the question would be Miguel Vargas or even fellow reliever Grant Taylor but after throwing three scoreless innings in Game 1 of the wild-card round, Smith is my X factor for the next one. -- Jesse Rogers

Cleveland Guardians

What carried the Guardians to an October bye?

They went 9-1 down the stretch to clinch the AL Central after trailing by as many as six games in the middle of August. From Aug. 18 to the clinching game, the Guardians went 25-11 with a 3.51 ERA. That will have to be the formula in the playoffs: pitching, pitching and more of it.

Rookie Parker Messick, who finished with a 2.56 ERA, and Gavin Williams, who led the AL with 248 strikeouts, guided the way, while closer Cade Smith topped all relievers in win probability added while saving 41 games and fanning 107 in 74 innings.

The offense was much better in the second half, with Steven Kwan hitting .352 with a .445 OBP in the final three months, but the pitching will be the key.

Why will it/won't it continue against the White Sox?

The Guardians will be the heavy favorite since they're rested with their rotation lined up while the White Sox lack the pitching depth of Cleveland's staff. Yes, the White Sox have more power -- Angel Martinez led the Guardians with 18 home runs -- but the Guardians did have their best power month in September, slugging .430 with 35 home runs in 25 games. Travis Bazzana, Brayan Rocchio, Chase DeLauter and Martinez all had good final months, so suddenly the Cleveland lineup looks playoff-worthy.

Which one player must deliver to put them in the ALCS?

It still feels like Jose Ramirez needs to offer big contributions at some point, something he hasn't done much of in the postseason in his Hall of Fame career. He has hit .234 with just four home runs in 45 career playoff games. If we focus on more recent years, he has hit .246 with two home runs in 19 games since 2022.

He has hit for very little power since returning from a fractured left hamate bone, managing only two home runs in 53 games after coming off the IL, but Stephen Vogt has still been hitting him second in the lineup down the stretch. That's a run-producing spot in the order and he'll need to produce some runs. -- David Schoenfield

stories.headline: Former Steelers HC Mike Tomlin reveals massive Minecraft city
stories.summary: The former Steelers coach revealed an unexpected longtime hobby that shocked the sports and gaming worlds.
stories.body:
Mike Tomlin is a Super Bowl-winning head coach, is second on the Pittsburgh Steelers' all-time wins list and famously never had a losing record in 19 seasons with the Steelers.

But on Wednesday, Tomlin showed a side of himself rarely seen: that of an architect. On Minecraft, to be exact.

Speaking about his passions for high-rise buildings and urban planning, Tomlin unveiled his Minecraft world in a nearly 20-minute YouTube video. Tomlin has been working on the ongoing project for 12-plus years.

After he watched his kids obsessively play the game in middle school, Tomlin became intrigued by the game's creative mode, which allows users to build cities with unlimited resources. The former head coach explains on the video that he likes to build and always had an interest in architecture.

It also became a way for Tomlin to spend time with his kids. Each of them participated and have buildings across the city.

"Over the course of time, they got just disinterested in the game. They go on to high school and so forth and off to college. Their participation became less and less over the years. My participation probably at times increased," Tomlin says, laughing. "At different times over the course of a 12-month calendar, I would have different levels of fixation on this."

He remembers constructing the various communities, neighborhoods and buildings with challenges along the way. But he describes the process of building his world as "mindless entertainment" and "therapeutic."

"I'm not a big TV watcher," he says. "It allowed me to detach from the realities and the pressures of life."

Tomlin shows off the various apartments and architecture, and he gives a tour of buildings, apologizing for his "lack of stick control" with a controller.

He also breaks down his vision for the city: densely populated buildings around a body of water. He started small before building neighborhoods over 12 years.

The first building Tomlin created is a "boutique hotel" that includes an executive spa and therapy rooms. He described himself as "lighting conscious" when building it, using glass ceilings when appropriate. The hotel includes indoor and outdoor boutiques, an elevator well and a main desk.

Another community within his city features an apartment building with an aquarium on each floor.

He says he was "view conscious" of the many high rises, making sure the high-end urban apartment buildings had great sightlines. One of them is right across from baseball and soccer stadiums, which Tomlin teases he'll reveal in another episode.

No detail was too small.

"You'll find appropriate number of public restrooms and stuff throughout all my public facilities, men's and women's restrooms," he says. "Not anything over the top in terms of detail ... but it was important that I represented that."

Tomlin's favorite rooftop penthouse includes the sign "Trump Tower" on the front. A caption ran underneath the video clarifying: "Not an endorsement. ... This build is [circa] 2015 ... we didn't think he would win ... TWICE."

Tomlin spawned villagers inside the building to "get a sense of how people moved throughout the space," which includes open living and dining spaces, a "Jack and Jill" bedroom design and a rooftop outdoor entertainment area.

He says that in the next episode he'll return with "something you'll find really interesting," though he didn't share when it would drop. Minecraft users beware.

Tomlin coached the Steelers for 19 seasons from 2007 to 2025, making him the NFL's longest-tenured head coach until he stepped down Jan. 13. He has since joined NBC Sports as an analyst.

stories.headline: Maple Leafs beat the Islanders 2-1 to rebound from opening loss
stories.summary: — Easton Cowan had a goal and an assist in the first period and the Toronto Maple Leafs beat the New York Islanders 2-1 on Wednesday night for their first victory under coach Jim Hiller.
stories.body:
TORONTO -- — Easton Cowan had a goal and an assist in the first period and the Toronto Maple Leafs beat the New York Islanders 2-1 on Wednesday night for their first victory under coach Jim Hiller.


The Maple Leafs rebounded from a 3-2 home loss to Montreal in their opener Tuesday night, spoiling the Islanders' first game of the season.


Colton Sissons also scored for Toronto, and Anthony Stolarz made 26 saves.


Emil Heineman scored in the third period for New York. Ilya Sorokin stopped 24 shots.


Sissons redirected his first goal for Toronto at 7:14 of the first period off Nick Paul's setup. Cowan then shoveled home a power-play rebound with 8:05 left in the period.


Reunited with fellow netminder Sergei Bobrovsky after winning the Stanley Cup together with Florida in 2024, Stolarz was perfect until Heineman scored short-handed with 5:51 left.


Up next
Islanders: Host New Jersey on Saturday night.


Maple Leafs: Host Ottawa on Saturday night.

stories.headline: WNBA playoffs 2026: How the Dream swept the Mystics
stories.summary: No. 4 seed Atlanta is back in the WNBA semifinals for the first time since 2018 after sweeping Washington.
stories.body:
One of the matchups in the WNBA semifinals is set. The Atlanta Dream secured their spot Wednesday as they swept the Washington Mystics with a 93-75 victory.

The No. 4 Dream will face the No. 8 New York Liberty in the semifinals. The Liberty knocked off the top-seeded Minnesota Lynx on Tuesday.

Atlanta, headed to its first semifinals since 2018, and New York are the only teams to advance so far. The Dream will host the Liberty on Sunday in Game 1 of the semifinals.

The No. 2 seed Golden State Valkyries can join them with a win over the 7-seed Dallas Wings. Game 2 of that series is underway on ESPN.

ESPN takes a look at how Atlanta advanced. Come back later for postgame analysis on Golden State-Dallas.

(4) Atlanta Dream 93, (5) Washington Mystics 75

How the game was won: Allisha Gray was the biggest factor for the Dream. The guard had a team-high 22 points and kept making big plays every time the Mystics threatened to come back. Point guard Jordin Canada also was key, finishing with 19 points, 11 assists and seven rebounds. The experience of the Dream's players vs. the Mystics was expected to be a factor in this series, and that's how it played out. Gray is in her 10th season and Canada is in her ninth, having won WNBA titles in 2018 and 2020 with Seattle. When the Dream needed to lock down in Games 1 and 2, the veterans knew how to do it.

In a foul-plagued game -- 53 combined -- Dream guard Rhyne Howard fouled out with 6:03 remaining in the game. She left with 15 points, but Atlanta didn't struggle without her. All five Dream starters finished in double figures. It wasn't surprising that the Dream lost the board battle; they were second to league-leading Washington in the regular season in rebounds per game. But the size of the rebounding margin -- 42-27 for the Mystics -- was a little surprising. Still, the Dream held the Mystics to 38% shooting and for the most part controlled the game, even if Washington stayed in it until Atlanta shut the door with a 28-17 edge in the fourth quarter.

What it means for the Dream: For the first time since 2018, the Dream are in the semifinals. They lost in the first round the last three years. Last season was particularly frustrating, because they lost Game 3 at home to Indiana. This year, they didn't let it get to a Game 3. While they trailed by five at halftime of Game 1, they owned the second half of that contest. A strong performance in back-to-back games sends them confidently into a matchup with the New York Liberty, who swept their first-round series against the top-seeded Minnesota Lynx.

The Liberty are the No. 8 seed, but this is a case where numbers are deceiving. New York had its ups and downs in the regular season, but no one really thought of the Liberty as a typical No. 8 seed. The Dream won the regular-season series 2-1, with the last two games coming in the final week of the season at New York. Atlanta won both, 95-84 on Sept. 21 and 83-65 on Sept. 23, although the Liberty's Breanna Stewart didn't play in that last game.

New York won its first WNBA title in 2024. Atlanta has been swept in all three of its WNBA Finals appearances (2010, 2011 and 2013).

What it means for the Mystics: As ESPN colleague Kareem Copeland said, the Mystics were playing with house money in this postseason. Lots of teams clamor to be underdogs, but Washington really was. At the start of the season, few picked the Mystics to make the playoffs, yet they ended up with the No. 5 seed. As the youngest team (by average age) in the WNBA, the Mystics are ahead of schedule. Most of their players had never appeared in the postseason before, and now they have that experience.

Center Shakira Austin, who moved into elite status in 2026, struggled in her final game of the season, finishing with nine points and three rebounds. But the entire season is something for her to build upon. Sonia Citron (25 points, seven rebounds) and Kiki Iriafen (15 points, 16 rebounds) did all they could Wednesday to extend the series. What a year it has been for that duo, who were the No. 3 and No. 4 picks of the 2025 draft. They not only helped get the Mystics back into the playoffs for the first time since 2023, but they also were part of the gold-medal-winning U.S. team at the FIBA Women's World Cup.

Iriafen just turned 23 last month, and Citron will be 23 on Oct. 22. Austin is 26. That is a young trio who Mystics fans should be excited to watch in 2027. -- Michael Voepel

The Indiana Fever kept their season alive. Can the Washington Mystics and Dallas Wings do the same Wednesday?

Both teams missed the WNBA playoffs the past two years but must take advantage of their home courts and win Wednesday to avoid being eliminated in the first round.

The No. 5 seed Mystics host the No. 4 Atlanta Dream (7 p.m. ET, ESPN) and the No. 7 Wings host the No. 2 Golden State Valkyries (9 p.m. ET, ESPN) in Game 2 of their best-of-three series.

In Sunday's playoff openers, the Mystics fell 92-77 at Atlanta, and the Wings lost 104-80 at Golden State. Washington led by five at halftime, but the game turned around with the Dream's huge 29-12 third-quarter surge. The Wings, prepared for the Valkyries' league-best defense, couldn't keep pace with Golden State's 18 3-pointers and franchise-record scoring total.

Sunday was the first playoff experience for five 2025 first-round draft picks: Dallas' Paige Bueckers and Aziaha James, and Washington's Sonia Citron, Kiki Iriafen and Georgia Amoore.

"This is the stage we want to be on," Iriafen said after Sunday's loss. "This is our first time being here. Not that that's an excuse, but now we know what it looks like. We have a taste for it. We'll be better prepared for our game on Wednesday."

The Mystics and Wings go in with the mission of beating the higher seed. Washington defeated Atlanta twice in the regular season, but Dallas lost three times to Golden State. Here's a look at what could determine Wednesday's results.

What must the Mystics do differently?
Voepel: First, cut down on turnovers, which really hurt them in Game 1. The Mystics had 22 turnovers to seven for Atlanta, with the Dream scoring 27 points off the giveaways to only four for the Mystics.

"They're a very physical team; they have good defenders," Citron said of the turnover issue. "We can't let them speed us up. It's kind of on us."

Overall, both teams played aggressive defense, but the Dream had the better of that, especially when they took control in the third quarter.

"I think we just let them get comfortable offensively," Citron said. "In the first half, we did a good job of just making everything hard for them. In that third quarter, we just let some of our discipline slip. Once they get going, it's really hard to stop them."

Washington did, though, in two out of three games in the regular season, beating the Dream 81-76 on July 2 and 79-74 on Aug. 7. Both games were at Washington, as opposed to the Mystics' 109-77 loss at Atlanta on June 6.

Coach Sydney Johnson said overall, the Mystics -- most of whom were appearing in their first playoff game -- performed pretty well. But that's not enough in the postseason.

"There's an elevated level of play in the playoffs," Johnson said. "I was really proud of how we met that. But we probably met it instead of initiating it in the third and fourth quarters."

What must the Wings do differently?
Andrews: The Wings need more from everyone not named Paige Bueckers. She had a historic night in her playoff debut, becoming the first player in WNBA history to shoot at least 90% from the field and score 20 points or more in her first postseason game. But no one else stepped up to help her. At halftime, Dallas' bench was scoreless and none of the other three players who had scored for the Wings had over six points. Yes, by the end of the game the Wings' second unit was outscored by only four points, but by then the game was decided.

"The score should not dictate your effort," Wings coach Jose Fernandez said after the game.

Jessica Shepard, a candidate for Most Improved Player, was held scoreless. The Valkyries have done a good job at keeping Shepard quiet in some of their previous matchups this season, but she still found other ways to influence the game. In Game 1, she lacked her usual impact on the boards and as a facilitator, finishing with three rebounds, three assists and three turnovers. Arike Ogunbowale and Awak Kuier will also need to produce more.

Bueckers said the Wings' lackluster offensive night also impacted their defense, something they need to change if they want to extend the series.

"We've been a team that has a bad habit of letting made or missed shots dictate how hard we play on the defensive end," Bueckers said. "This is the playoffs, so it's really unacceptable."

What's at stake for the Dream and the Valkyries?
Voepel: Atlanta last made the semifinals in 2018, then missed the playoffs the next four seasons. The Dream returned to the playoffs in 2023 behind Rhyne Howard, the 2022 No. 1 pick, and Allisha Gray, who came to Atlanta that year in a trade from Dallas. They've been the Dream's scoring leaders in all four of their seasons together in Atlanta. But first-round playoff exits the past three years have been a disappointment.

The Dream were swept by Dallas in 2023 and by New York in 2024. Last season against Indiana, the Dream won their first-round opener at home, then lost the next two games and the series.

"The next game is going to be hard," Howard said of Wednesday's matchup in Washington. "They're going to want to come out with more aggression. What we did in the first half, we can't have happen again."

The Valkyries, meanwhile, are in only their second season of existence, but they are ahead of schedule for the average expansion team in pro sports. Last season, as the No. 8 seed, they were swept by Minnesota in the first round.

After shutting down the Wings' inside game Sunday, the Valkyries know that will probably be a point of emphasis for Dallas to greatly improve on in Game 2. And as good as Golden State's offense looked in Game 1, the Valkyries generally do not want high-scoring battles. If they win and close out the series, it might be a very different game than the opener.

Andrews: Before the Valkyries even left the court in Game 1, coach Natalie Nakase's staff was already talking strategy for Game 2. They know the Wings will make adjustments, and they also can't necessarily expect them to have as historic of a shooting night in Game 2. But the Valkyries feel extremely confident.

Golden State's defensive mindset has been one of the most unshakable identities in the WNBA this season, and that's not changing now. Even after Bueckers scored 21 points on 9-of-10 shooting, the Valkyries were pleased with their approach.

"She's an excellent player, one of the best in the league," Christyn Williams said. "As long as I can make [her shots] hard, where she has to really work for them, she will get tired. That's the goal. She's going to get them, but how can I wear her down?"

Golden State remains a young and relatively inexperienced team in the greater landscape of the league, but Veronica Burton said the Valkyries do not feel like underdogs. They were unhappy that last year's playoff appearance (a first-round sweep) "ended as quickly as it started," Burton said, so they don't want to give Dallas the opportunity to take away this series.

-->

stories.headline: St. Louis up to 2nd place with unbeaten run now at 17 games
stories.summary: Simon Becher and Tomas Ostrak each scored late in the second half as St. Louis City SC beat the New York Red Bulls 3-0 on Wednesday night.
stories.body:
Simon Becher and Tomas Ostrak each scored late in the second half as St. Louis City SC beat the New York Red Bulls 3-0 on Wednesday night.

St. Louis (13-6-8) extended its unbeaten streak to 17 matches in MLS play and moved up to second place in MLS' Western Conference table.

New York (9-12-6) entered having conceded just two goals in its last four games, with Ethan Horvath recording three shutouts.

The Red Bulls had won their last two games, but were without rising stars Adri Mehmeti and Julian Hall for the game, with the pair away on national team duty for the United States.

Rafael Navarro opened the scoring just five minutes into the game when he redirected Conrad Wallem's header across the goal.

Becher capitalized on a New York turnover deep in its own half to make it 2-0 in the 87th minute. Ostrak sent in a rebound in stoppage time.

Roman Bürki made four saves to earn his third clean sheet of the season for St. Louis.

It was the first time New York and St. Louis have met during the regular season.

St. Louis hosts the LA Galaxy next on Oct. 11, while the Red Bulls play San Diego FC at home the day before.

stories.headline: 76ers guard Tyrese Maxey: 'I want to be judged by winning'
stories.summary: Coming off a career year, Tyrese Maxey said he doesn't want to be judged by how he does individually but by how the 76ers do as a team this year.
stories.body:
CAMDEN, N.J. -- Having earned two All-Star nods in the last three seasons and coming off a campaign in which he averaged a career-high 28.3 points per game, Philadelphia 76ers guard Tyrese Maxey is primed for another big year.

But the 25-year-old said Wednesday after the Sixers' second practice of training camp that the only metric he cares about for Philadelphia's highly anticipated upcoming season is team success.

"I'm at the point now where I've showed what I can do talent-wise," Maxey said. "Of course, I'm going to continue to get better, but I want to be judged by winning. If we win, that's what I want to be judged by. That's really my main mindset, my main goal, is finding ways to win."

Maxey was the first of Philly's four major stars -- including Joel Embiid, Jaylen Brown and LeBron James -- to speak to reporters since training camp started Tuesday.

Brown sidestepped a query on media day Monday when asked about how the Sixers will determine a pecking order and identify an "alpha" by replying: "Next question."

Maxey's answer was in the same spirit, albeit much more elaborate, as he detailed his willingness to adjust to help the team.

"Because I've played so many different roles, I'm capable of doing so many different things," Maxey said. "And I think that's going to be a positive for myself and for this team. I can play on the ball. I can play off the ball. I can play in transition. I can catch and shoot. Play off [of] pin downs. I can play pick-and-roll. ...

"I'm going to play however they need me to play. However Coach [Nick Nurse] wants to play, that's how I'm going to play."

And Maxey is not only leading by example. He is speaking up as the new group gets off the ground.

"My voice carries a little bit and then just the charisma of me smiling and having a good time," Maxey said. "I mean, I'm getting older ... and I just feel like I've been here for a minute. Process [Embiid] has been here, I think what, 13 years? I've been here seven. So, we've been here for a while, kind of know how things go around here and just am trying to keep using my voice and help everybody get familiar and help everybody get comfortable."

Beyond vowing to acquiesce to any role change that is asked of him, Maxey also used his voice to be effusive in his praise of the other stars on the team in his answers Wednesday.

On James: "That's like a big brother to me. He's an old man ... He's a good guy. He's a good guy."

On Embiid: "He looks amazing. He looks happy. ... When you're healthy and you're happy and you're at peace with your life and basketball, that's when you're at your best. He's been great."

On Brown: "JB's like physically a freak of nature. He's just stronger than you. He jumps higher than you. He's faster than you and he's very talented. Those are the things that you see every single day. And I think what's stood out to me so far is his communication and he's willing to pick up the ball defensively, kind of just do whatever coach needs him to do right now."

Brown was the last player on the court after practice, working on handling double teams in the post - by kicking out to a shooter or fading away for a jumper along the baseline - with a massive Sixers logo on the wall of the practice facility behind him.

Maxey made sure to acknowledge the transition for Brown, too, as he begins life with the Sixers after having played for the Boston Celtics for his entire career before being traded within the Atlantic Division in July.

"This is very foreign to him, imagine being somewhere for [10] years and coming here, the team that you're trained to hate, probably," Maxey said. "It's been great. Especially [since] we just beat [Boston in the playoffs]. It's kind of crazy."

stories.headline: Ayrton Senna's Honda NSX could fetch £800,000 at London auction
stories.summary: A 1991 Honda NSX that once belonged to Ayrton Senna will go up for auction in London at the end of October.
stories.body:
A 1991 Honda NSX that once belonged to Ayrton Senna will go up for auction in London at the end of October.

Chassis number T000233 was one of three NSXs delivered to Senna as part of his contract with Honda in the early 1990s and, due to its provenance, carries an estimate of £500,000 to £800,000.

When the car first went on sale in 1990 it had a list price of between £52,000 and £55,000, with low-mileage NSXs from the same era currently listed online for up to £135,000.

The legendary Japanese sports car is closely linked to Senna, who contributed to its development before it went on sale as Honda's answer to the more expensive Porsche and Ferrari sportscars of the era.

Chassis T000233 is finished in Formula Red over a black leather interior and was delivered to Portugal in March 1991 so that Senna could make use of it while staying at his property in Quinta do Lago.

According to the listing on Sotheby's website, the NSX featured in the 1992 documentary, 'Ayrton Senna: Racing Is In My Blood' and was used by the Brazilian to commute to the 1991 Portuguese Grand Prix in Estoril.

Senna, who died in an accident at the 1994 San Marino Grand Prix, won all three of his world titles with Honda power while racing at McLaren.

stories.headline: Former draftee slams AFL over concussion plight
stories.summary: An AFL draftee whose life was upended by a concussion injury says he "was so close to ending everything".
stories.body:
An AFL draftee whose life was upended by a concussion injury says he "was so close to ending everything".

Aiden O'Driscoll, who had to retire because of a devastating training injury without making his AFL debut, also slammed the league as an "absolute joke".

"The last couple of years I've experienced nothing but pain, and I've explained it multiple times to you. You're supposed to help AFL players through hardship, not leave them with absolutely nothing," O'Driscoll wrote in his extensive Instagram post.

His comments came a day after Geelong announced defender Jake Kolodjashnij had retired.

Last month, the Cats were fined $140,000 and current AFL chairman Craig Drummond apologised after it emerged the club had agreed to a secret concussion waiver with Kolodjashnij. Drummond was Geelong president at the time the agreement was struck.

The Geelong controversy highlighted the complexity and sensitivity around contact sport's concussion crisis.

The Western Bulldogs recruited O'Driscoll in the 2023 draft. But a head injury that summer left him with significant ongoing health problems and the club announced in May, 2024 that he had retired on medical grounds.

"The doctors described my concussion as 'one of the worst' they've seen, with eight micro brain bleeds, and (a) fracture behind my ear," O'Driscoll wrote.

"From a medical point of view, losing my career, my identity plus going through the symptoms I have, you'd think the AFL would be useful with some support?

O'Driscoll added it took the AFL six weeks to find him a psychologist.

"Through this period, I was grieving the most, it got to the point where I started questioning my life? If it was worth living?," he wrote.

"I was so close to ending everything, I would've been free from all the pain/trauma. My family/close friends and partners honestly kept me here."

Melbourne premiership player Angus Brayshaw also had to retire in 2024 because of his concussion issues.

In his emotional toast to other retiring players at the Brownlow Medal function that year, Brayshaw referred to O'Driscoll by name.

"I know a few other past players that are dealing with the same issues as I am," O'Driscoll said.

"AFL it's time to step up! I'm a 21-year-old that can't keep suffering each week. While you're at it, help the other past players that need support."

O'Driscoll added he had been told at 18 never to play contact sport again.

The AFL and the players' association were contacted for comment.

stories.headline: This means so much to Newcastle: Knights fans explain 25 years of frustration
stories.summary: The Knights were going to a Grand Final for the first time in a quarter of a century, and it's enough to make a grown man cry.
stories.body:
When Sandon Smith intercepted a pass during a final desperate Panthers raid and raced 80 metres to seal a preliminary final victory for Newcastle, Accor Stadium erupted, women and children screamed, and grown men sobbed. The Knights were going to a Grand Final for the first time in a quarter of a century.

Across the Hunter region, people started decorating their homes with streamers, flags and jerseys, some painted their houses blue and red. A sense of communal joy united people who had endured so much rugby league frustration over the 25 years since Andrew Johns put on a clinic to upset the Eels in the 2001 decider.

The Knights first entered the competition in 1988 and stuck loyal to the ARL during the relatively brief, but tumultuous Super League war. In 1997 with the game torn in two, the Knights won their first title defeating Manly in one of the most memorable Grand Finals ever played. Four years later when they conquered Parramatta, no one expected it would be so painfully long before their next shot at the title.

Through the 25 years the crowds still packed the home stadium, the fans endured four wooden spoons along the way, but never wavered. If anything it strengthened their resolve, the perseverance required to be a Knights fan was something to be proud of.

ESPN spoke to four Newcastle fans of various ages and experiences to see what this Grand Final really means to them.

Nick an 18-year-old in his final year of school, who wasn't even born when the Knights last saluted. Adam and Tim who were in their teens back in the glory days, and Derek who remembers the early struggles, the sunburnt glory of 1997 and the joy of 2001.

Why do you love rugby league and more importantly why are you a Knights fan?
Nick 18, of Rouse Hill: I've been around rugby league since I was six years old. Being involved as a player, coach and commentator, it has given me the opportunity and ability to understand the game, not just as a game, but also everything that goes into it. This has helped me understand the impact of Holbrook's coaching style and the impact of a fan base and a city on the team. My love for the Knights stems from my family's history in the city. They were living there supporting Wests Newcastle back before the Knights were added in 1988.

Adam 43, of Old Toongabbie: I love the combative nature of rugby league. I grew up on the Central Coast, so the Knights were the team I followed as they were closest to where I lived, but growing up in the era of Joey Johns and our first premierships made it an easy choice.

Tim 41, of Terrigal: To be honest, I don't think I ever really had a choice. I grew up in Western Sydney, where rugby league wasn't just a sport - it was a way of life. I started playing when I was seven years of age, and at home, Friday nights meant gathering around the TV to watch the footy, and Sunday afternoons were reserved for more of the same. All I wanted to do was play footy, watch footy, and talk footy. For me, rugby league is about the mates I've shared the game with, and the love of a sport that has always been part of my life. Why the Knights? My family had a caravan at Swansea, and while other families might have packed up and headed to the beach in summer, we would head up to the caravan in winter. And what happens in winter? There I was, spending my winters around Swansea, and watching the Newcastle Knights. Before I knew it, those red-and-blue colours had worked their way into my system and the timing couldn't have been better. That was the 1990s - the golden era of Newcastle rugby league!

Derek 53, of Green Point: I love the game and the skills required to play it. Being born a Novocastrian, I have supported them since they entered the competition in 1988.

What does it mean to you to have the Knights in this Grand Final?
Nick: It means more than anything. From last year's wooden spoon and all the injuries this year, the way the city has reacted says it all.

Adam: It feels kind of surreal to me still. From where we were last season and the feeling I had at the end of the year, I was fairly despondent and not enjoying watching league due to how the Knights were travelling. I told my son Harvey (8-years-old) that I wasn't sure if I could keep following them. He encouraged me to keep going, he knew how much I loved watching them. I'm certainly glad he did, as this year has been awesome!

Tim: Honestly? RELIEF! ABSOLUTE, UNBELIEVABLE RELIEF! After 25 years of patience, pain, false hope, and wondering whether I'd ever see the Newcastle Knights back on the biggest stage, we're finally here. Twenty-five years! That's not just supporting a football team - that's a long-term emotional commitment that probably deserves some sort of compensation package. There's something incredibly special about seeing the Knights in the Grand Final. It's relief, it's pride, it's nostalgia, and most importantly, it's the chance to finally enjoy being a Knights supporter without having to explain why we're sitting near the bottom of the ladder again. After 25 years and four wooden spoons, one thing is certain; we've earned the right to enjoy this moment.

Derek: It's a fantastic achievement given the run of injuries and the number of games we lost by two points or less this season. It takes me back to 1997 and 2001 where we went on runs as underdogs to win. All Knights supporters have been through a lot over the last 25 years as we moved away from the foundations of what made our club great and the style of play that made us proud. It's great that a number of local juniors have been brought through over the past few years.

How did you react to the Knights beating the Panthers?
Nick: It didn't feel real. But, the whole season I felt it coming, I kept saying a healthy Knights team wins the comp.

Adam: Harvey and I were at the game! After halftime we spoke about maybe leaving early if we were being blown away, being down to 12 players. To see how we started the second half, it just felt like were we going to win after the Dom Young try. To see my son, who is a massive Eels fan, be so happy to support the team I follow, to having tears of happiness at the end of the Panthers game, sums up how much it meant to me!

Tim: Honestly, I knew we could win, but in my wildest dreams, I never expected it to happen the way it did. Let's be honest, when you're a Knights supporter, you learn to manage your expectations. Beating the Panthers? A team that's been the benchmark of the competition for years? That was something else entirely. I knew we had a chance, Nathan Cleary was on the bench, Blaize Talagi was opposite Bradman Best, but to actually get the job done against a team of that quality? There's something particularly satisfying about beating the best. My reaction to the win was tears of joy and pride in the team.

Derek: Tears.

What do you remember about the 1997 and 2001 victories?
Nick: Well I wasn't alive, but rewatching the Darren Albert try and the videos from Newcastle that night, still gives me goosebumps.

Adam: I was showing Harvey the highlights of these matches last night. The 1997 Grand Final stands out most to me as I was in Melbourne for a tennis tournament, but I was glued to the TV. I recall jumping around and fist pumping for the next hour.

Tim: What I remember most is just how much the whole city of Newcastle got behind the Knights. You couldn't escape the excitement - everyone was talking about them, and you could feel that something special was happening. One of the memories that really sticks with me is seeing people lining the streets waving the team bus goodbye. It showed just how much the team meant to Newcastle. It wasn't just a football team - they were representing the whole city, and everyone wanted to be part of the journey. I can still remember the absolute explosion of emotion when Darren Albert crossed the line in 1997 and the brilliance of Joey Johns' 2001 Grand Final masterclass. Those two victories weren't just premierships, they were moments when the whole of Newcastle came together, and all the memories are still incredibly special.

Derek: The belief instilled by Paul Harragon and the Johns brothers, and the never-say-die attitude in not only the Grand Finals but in the lead-up games. This year is particularly similar to the '97 build-up, where we were behind in games and won in the dying stages.

Where will you be watching this one?
Nick: I didn't get tickets to the game, so I'll be watching it with my mates. I'm hoping to rub it in to some Roosters fans.

Adam: I will be in Gloucester with my family for our annual long weekend get away. We'll be having Chinese at the local bowling club, where they'll have the big screen set up and the joint will be packed out (at least 100 people) to cheer on the Knights to victory!

Tim: Well given that we finished 2025 in last place, I booked a family trip to Japan, thinking we were no chance of making the 2026 Grand Final. As a result, I will be watching the Grand Final at the Pig and Whistle British pub in Kyoto, Japan.

Derek: At home.

Favourite all-time Knights player?
Nick: Paul "Chief" Harragon. I think it goes without saying, the guy is Newcastle

Adam: I absolutely loved Robbie O [O'Davis] back in the day, but it's hard to go past Joey [Andrew Johns]. It's not just was he did on the field, but his continued love for the Knights and the way he shows his emotions during both the tough and good times.

Tim: Andrew Johns.

Derek: Andrew "Joey" Johns, with Mark Hughes a close second.

Favourite current player?
Nick: Trey Mooney, the guy loves his footy. He does the hard work, runs a good line and is just a really good footballer. He is the guy you want on your team.

Adam: Bradman Best is the man I like seeing with time and space. This year I have found so many great players within our squad. The exciting part is how young a lot of them are, that gives me more encouragement for the years to come as well.

Tim: Kalyn Ponga.

Derek: "Frank the Tank" - Francis Manuleleua.

What has coach Holbrook changed that has turned the Knights around so quickly?
Nick: The culture and the attack. As a former player, he understands what the Knights' badge means. The way he has altered the attack to fit the way the team plays. Everything he does works.

Adam: He has understood the strengths within our team. The statistic that stood out most this year was tries from our 50. Last year we scored three, up until the finals this year it was 53. Also the resolve that has been built across the entire season. This has been generated from lessons learnt throughout the various situations the Knights have been in, but drawn on when needed the most.

Tim: He has connected the team to the city. He has also invented a new style of rugby league. The focus is shifting to the edges and allowing our back five to do their thing. Whilst most teams focus on their middles, the Knights challenge both edges, and often. We have one of the best 1-7 line-ups and Holbrook has created a plan that suits these strengths.

Derek: Attack and creativity, confidence and defensive resolve. Getting the Knights back to the DNA that made them successful.

How much would victory in this Grand Final mean to you?
Nick: You can't put it into words. A trip up the M1 would be imminent just to enjoy the moment. To see a trophy in my lifetime would feel unreal.

Adam: Each round of the finals I've entered the game with optimism and a sense of excitement for what I was about to witness, all the while proud of what already has been achieved. But bringing the premiership back to Newcastle will change lives for not only the players, but maybe more so the fans.

Tim: As mentioned earlier, I have waited 25 years to see the Knights in another Grand Final. I was 16 years of age when we last won one. I couldn't help but tear up last Sunday. I'm sure more will follow if we win. Bring on the Roosters. I'm quietly confident our edges will get the job done again.

Derek: It would be great for the city and our family and in particular the New Lambton community. A great reward to the players and the fans who supported them through the tough times. It would also be a reward for previous coaches like Rick Stone and Nathan Brown who had the helm in our darkest days and began the rebuild, including attracting Kalyn to the club, with no promise of success.

The Philadelphia Phillies started things off with yet another dramatic comeback win to even the series against the Atlanta Braves and force Game 3. The Chicago White Sox followed that up with a sweep of the Houston Astros to become the first wild-card team to move on to the division series. Next up: The New York Yankees knocked out their rival Boston Red Sox from the postseason with a second straight blowout win.

New York Yankees 9, Boston Red Sox 2
New York wins series 2-0

It was over when ... Red Sox ace Garrett Crochet struck out Spencer Jones ... and didn't record an out. Pitching for the first time since late April due to left-shoulder issues, Crochet came on in relief in the sixth inning with Boston facing a 2-1 deficit. He got an atrocious swing from Jones on a sweeper in the dirt, and after the ball kicked away, Red Sox catcher Adley Rutschman was slow in retrieving the ball and firing it to first base. Jones, originally called out, was deemed safe after replay, setting the stage for the biggest inning so far of the postseason. Three singles later, Crochet was out, and four batters after that, Cody Bellinger followed an intentional walk to Ben Rice with a three-run homer to cap the six-run frame. It all started with the out that wasn't -- and ended Boston's season in grim fashion. -- Jeff Passan

Stat that defined the game: To win this series, the Yankees' left-handed hitters needed to produce against left-handed pitching. The Red Sox carried five left-handed relievers -- plus left-handed starters for Games 1 and 3. The Yankees' best hitters -- with Aaron Judge left off the roster and Giancarlo Stanton limited to pinch-hitting duties -- are left-handed. It was Boston's path to victory. The strategy worked in neither contest. In Game 2, Yankees left-handed hitters went 4-for-6 against left-handed relievers Erik Miller and Garrett Crochet between the fifth and sixth innings, which set the stage for Cody Bellinger's three-run home run off right-hander Garrett Whitlock to blow the game open. Yankees left-handed hitters finished the series 11-for-22 with a 1.182 OPS against lefties. The success fueled the club's 18-run explosion. -- Jorge Castillo

It was over when ... Chase Meidroth took Bryan Abreu deep for a back-breaking three-run blast in the sixth. This came just minutes after it looked like Houston was about to overcome Chicago's early 4-0 edge. With two on in the fifth inning and the lead down to 4-3, Anthony Kay came out of the bullpen to get Yordan Alvarez on a fly to left. After a walk to Isaac Paredes loaded the bases, Jose Altuve flied out to end the threat. After the White Sox drew two walks to start the sixth, Meidroth showed bunt on Abreu's first two offerings. Following a double steal, Meidroth went back to swing mode and launched what turned out to be a series-clinching blast. The White Sox's Cinderella ride continues into the American League Division Series.

Stat that defined the game: Alvarez managed just a lone single in eight at-bats during the brief series, a .125 average to go with some failings in high-leverage spots. He also failed to make a grab on a well-struck Sam Antonacci drive to start the game, something a more mobile left fielder might have caught. Alvarez is still great and on his way to win the AL MVP Award. But it was a rough couple of days for him in the wild-card round. -- Bradford Doolittle

It was over when ... It appeared to be over when Bryce Harper misplayed Drake Baldwin's relatively routine fly ball that turned into a generously-scored RBI single in the seventh inning to give the Braves a 2-1 lead (and they added another run). But then Kyle Schwarber and Harper hit back-to-back home runs in the eighth off Dylan Lee, who hadn't allowed a home run all season to a left-handed batter. Alec Bohm then hit the game-winning home run in the 10th off Didier Fuentes -- just Bohm's second opposite-field home run all season.

And then it was actually finally over when Andrew Painter struck out Dominic Smith with two runners on in the bottom of the 10th -- on a walk-off challenge on the third strike. The Phillies' season is alive.

Star who defined the game: The Phillies getting to Lee was the big shocker to begin with, and Bohm going to right field was also a shock, but the biggest shocker might have been Painter pitching the scoreless eighth, ninth and 10th innings for the Phillies. With Jhoan Duran having thrown 27 pitches on Tuesday and manager Don Mattingly not trusting anybody else in the bullpen -- which had the worst ERA in the majors in September -- he turned to his rookie, who had started in 23 of his 25 appearances. stories.headline: Allisha Gray leads Dream past Mystics, into WNBA semifinals
stories.summary: Allisha Gray scored 22 points, Jordin Canada had 13 of her 19 points in the fourth quarter, and the Dream advanced to the semifinals of the WNBA playoffs for the first time since 2018, beating the Mystics 93-75 in Game 2.
stories.body:
WASHINGTON -- Allisha Gray scored 22 points, Jordin Canada had 13 of her 19 points in the fourth quarter, and the Atlanta Dream advanced to the semifinals of the WNBA playoffs for the first time since 2018, beating the Washington Mystics 93-75 in Game 2 of their first-round series Wednesday night.

Atlanta, which had lost in the first round in each of the past three seasons, will host Game 1 of the semifinals on Sunday against New York, which swept Minnesota to become the first No. 8 seed to eliminate a No. 1 seed in the league's 30-year history.

Canada made 3-pointers on back-to-back possessions in the fourth quarter, and she added a jumper from the free throw line on Atlanta's next trip for an 89-70 lead with 2:58 left.

Canada also had 11 assists and seven rebounds. Rhyne Howard finished with 15 points before fouling out with 6:03 left in the fourth quarter. Angel Reese also had 15 points and Naz Hillmon added 10.

Sonia Citron scored 25 points for Washington. Kiki Iriafen had 15 points and 16 rebounds and became the first player in franchise history to have a first-half double-double in a playoff game.

Atlanta led 41-28 with 1:26 left in the first half before Washington closed on a 7-0 run, capped by Citron's shot in the lane just before the buzzer. The Mystics were hurt by 11 first-half turnovers.

Washington went on a 14-2 run starting in the third quarter to get to within 65-62. But Atlanta scored the next 13 points, capped by a 3-pointer by Canada, to rebuild a double-digit lead at 78-62.

The Mystics were making their first playoff appearance since winning the 2019 WNBA championship.

stories.headline: Philadelphia Union, USMNT's Cavan Sullivan becomes youngest MLS Player of the Month
stories.summary: Philadelphia Union and USMNT midfielder Cavan Sullivan became the youngest player in MLS history to be named Player of the Month on Wednesday when he was awarded the honors for September.
stories.body:
Philadelphia Union and United States men's national team midfielder Cavan Sullivan became the youngest player in MLS history to be named Player of the Month on Wednesday when he was awarded the honors for September.

At 16, Cavan Sullivan became the youngest player to start a game for the United States since Freddy Adu in 2006 when he was picked in Mauricio Pochettino's XI for Saturday's 4-1 friendly win vs. Peru.

He was one of 11 players -- including seven other teenagers -- to make their first appearances for the U.S. in that game against Peru.

Sullivan, who turned 17 on Sept. 28, came on as a substitute on Tuesday in the USMNT's 4-2 friendly win over Chile.

Sullivan has seven goals and 12 assists in 26 games for the Union, who have surged up to sixth place in the Eastern Conference in recent weeks. He has played 1,675 league minutes in MLS.

His 19 goal contributions are tied with Alphonso Davies (2018) for the second-most by a teenager in an MLS season, trailing only Diego Fagundez (20 in 2013).

Since returning from the World Cup break, the Union have recorded 32 points during a 12-game unbeaten streak, which is tied for the most points by a club in a 12-game span in MLS history. Sullivan has started all 11 of those games, logging a goal contribution in eight of them.

Sullivan and the Union will return after the FIFA international break on Oc. 10 to host Real Salt Lake at Subaru Park (7:30 p.m. ET).

stories.headline: Klopp not preparing for more titles after verdict against Man City
stories.summary: Jürgen Klopp said Wednesday he would "wait and see" before commenting on the Premier League's announcement yesterday that Manchester City had been found guilty of 114 charges for breaching financial rules.
stories.body:
Jürgen Klopp said Wednesday he would wait to see how things pan out before commenting on the Premier League's announcement yesterday that Manchester City had been found guilty of 114 charges for breaching financial rules.

The charges cover a period between 2009 and 2018, with Klopp's tenure at Liverpool -- which began in 2015 -- overlapping with the time that City were have found to be guilty of breaking Premier League rules.

On the eve of Germany's match against Serbia in the Nations League, though, Klopp seemed content to let his record at Merseyside speak for itself instead of speculating over what might have been.

"I haven't given it much thought, even though I've seen it of course," Klopp said. "Should any sanctions be imposed, I naturally have nothing to do with it anyway, and that's why I'm waiting to see how things pan out. But when you're talking about legal proceedings that have been going on for so long now, I assume there will be an appeal or something like that? That will take ages again of course.

"So I'm a long way from preparing myself for it in any way and I don't have any feelings about it."

City, who won the Premier League three times between 2009 and 2018, have denied all of the charges and are set to lodge an appeal against the verdict.

Of his longtime rival and Man City coach Pep Guardiola, Klopp said: "I also know what I said about it in the past and how if there's ever a parade, I'll be there. But it doesn't feel like that anymore. My respect for Pep Guardiola and the football played at City during the time we played against each other, in the way they played back then and how they brought football to life on the pitch -- plus what an opponent they proved to be for us at the very highest level -- is far too great for me to be able to say anything now."

Klopp was also tight-lipped on Germany's captain for the Nations League tie -- his third match in charge of the national team. The new Germany coach has a completely new squad to work with after he selected two groups for the four fixtures during this international window.

With regular captain Joshua Kimmich allowed to leave the camp after he featured in a 1-1 draw in the Netherlands and the shock home loss to Greece, Klopp must decide who wears the armband for this clash in Munich.

"The team will be led onto the pitch tomorrow by the player with the most international caps," Klopp said on Wednesday.

Captain question aside, Klopp did hint that Bayern Munich goalkeeper Jonas Urbig would play at his home stadium of Allianz Arena.

"Feel free to ask 'who might be a captaincy option,' but I don't reveal the starting lineup now. You can look them up yourselves," said Klopp. "I can only say that Jonas Urbig won't wear the armband in his first international match."

Urbig took part in a news conference after Klopp and expressed his delight at making his Germany debut.

"It's a moment you've worked towards your whole life and I'm simply delighted to have the opportunity tomorrow to play here in our own stadium and do my part to help us as a team achieve our first victory," Urbig said. "This No. 1 topic isn't something I'm concerned with. My focus is really on reaching my limit every day and pushing it even further. And everything else will perhaps fall into place over time."

Germany are without a win in four fixtures after a World Cup last-32 exit to Paraguay followed a group-stage loss to Ecuador, but Serbia are on an equally poor run.

Serbia have lost both Nations League fixtures by a 2-1 score to the Netherlands and Greece, respectively, after they suffered heavy defeats to Cape Verde and Mexico during the summer.

"Serbia's approach won't be much different from what Greece did. What makes Serbia particularly difficult to play against is their experience," Klopp said. "They also have some excellent footballers. They know all the tricks of the trade, so we have to be prepared for that.

"It's not the best period in Serbian football at the moment, but the players themselves know what's at stake. An opponent that sits deep is a major challenge for any team, at any stage of development."

Following the game against Serbia on Thursday, Germany will close out Nations League play for the September/October international window with a second match against Greece, this time in Thessaloniki on Oct. 4.
